Your Docker Compose stacks, updated step by step.

Palier reads the release notes of every version it skips, plans the upgrade, verifies each step with Docker and goes back to the last good step if something breaks.

Install Palier See how it works

Bumping a tag is the easy part

What breaks a self-hosted stack is everything around the tag. All of it is written in the release notes, and Palier reads them for you.

A required version was skipped
Palier follows every required stop, and refuses a plan that skips one.
The Compose file has to change
It removes the service, renames the variable or swaps the image the notes name, and nothing else: the operations come from a closed list.
The database changes major version
PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB move by export and reimport on a new volume, compared table by table. The old volume is never touched.
A dependency goes further than the application supports
The stack follows its application: a database or a cache goes no higher than what the application says it supports.
Something fails in the middle
Each step has its own restore point. The whole stack goes back to the last verified step, even after a power cut.
Old images pile up on the disk
Once a run is verified, the images it replaced are removed. Docker keeps the ones a container still uses.

One run, start to finish

The log of a run on the bench, unattended: Outline, its PostgreSQL moved from 16 to 18 by export and reimport, then its Redis. Seven minutes.

00:25:22 step 1 of 3: outline 1.10.1 to 1.13.0
00:28:33 step 2 of 3: postgres 16.4 to 18.6
00:28:41 export of postgres done: 129760 bytes, roles 1, databases 2, tables 42, rows 325, indexes 177, constraints 177
00:28:47 reimport verified, identical to the export: roles 1, databases 2, tables 42, rows 325, indexes 177, constraints 177
00:31:00 step 3 of 3: redis 7.2.4 to 8.10.3
00:32:19 result: completed

What happens between two versions

The AI proposes, the code decides. A plan that fails one check is never applied.

  1. InventoryThe Compose stacks of the machine, their images, volumes and dependencies.
  2. VersionsWhat the registry has that is newer, once it has matured for 72 hours.
  3. NotesEvery release note in between, read one by one, and the security advisories.
  4. PlanSteps made of operations from a closed list. The AI never writes a command.
  5. ValidationEach claim must quote a note word for word. The code rejects the rest.
  6. ApplyStep by step, with a restore point of the whole stack before each one.
  7. VerificationWhat Docker reports: running, stable, healthy. Then the next step.

Proven on real applications

Every feature is played in a virtual machine with a real Docker before it ships. These ran without anyone watching.

ApplicationPathWhat it took
GitLab CE16.1.6 → 19.5.113 required stops, waiting for the background migrations at each one. 3 h 43.
Immichv1.105.1 → v3.4.1128 release notes read one by one, a service removed, the database image replaced. 12 steps, same photos.
Outline1.10.1 → 1.13.0PostgreSQL 16 to 18 by export and reimport, Redis 7 to 8. 3 steps, 7 minutes.
n8n and its task runners2.45.7 → 3.2.2Two images of one release, moved in the same step.
A machine killed mid-upgradeGitLab, step 2 of 4The host ran out of memory. On restart, Palier put the stack back at the last verified step on its own.

One container, the Docker socket

No agent, no account. Start it next to your stacks. It applies what passes every check on its own; set PALIER_AUTO=off to approve each plan yourself.
